q: The groups of atoms that are attached to the carbon backbone of organic compounds are known as functional groups.
e: True. The groups of atoms that are attached to the carbon backbone of organic compounds are known as functional groups. Kb is the base dissociation constant; larger Kb means a stronger weak base.

q: An alkane lacks functional groups whereas an alkene and an alkyne have functional groups which are carbon-carbon double bond and carbon-carbon triple bond, respectively.
e: True. An alkane lacks functional groups whereas an alkene and an alkyne have functional groups which are carbon-carbon double bond and carbon-carbon triple bond, respectively. Ka is the acid dissociation constant; larger Ka means a stronger weak acid.

q: A chemical test is typically a fast reaction performed in a test tube that gives a visual clue as evidence for a chemical reaction.
e: True. A chemical test is typically a fast reaction performed in a test tube that gives a visual clue as evidence for a chemical reaction. The direction of this chemical relationship is the one chemists actually measure.

q: Alkynes pass through ammoniacal $Cu_2Cl_2$ solution to form a red coloured precipitate.
e: True. Alkynes pass through ammoniacal Cu2Cl2 solution to form a red coloured precipitate. The direction of this chemical relationship is the one chemists actually measure.

q: Alcohols turn the orange colour of acidified $K_2Cr_2O_7$ solution to green colour when warmed.
e: True. Alcohols turn the orange colour of acidified K2Cr2O7 solution to green colour when warmed. The direction of this chemical relationship is the one chemists actually measure.

q: Ethers are boiled with HI and then react with $AgNO_3$ to form a white coloured precipitate.
e: False. Ether cleavage with HI gives an alkyl iodide that can then give a yellow AgI precipitate, not a white AgCl-type solid. White would suggest chloride.

q: Aldehydes form a reddish-brown coloured precipitate when heated gently with Fehling's solution.
e: True. Aldehydes form a reddish-brown coloured precipitate when heated gently with Fehling's solution. An aldehyde has a carbonyl carbon attached to at least one hydrogen.

q: Ketones form a deep-orange coloured precipitate when mixed with 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine (2,4-DNP) solution.
e: True. Ketones form a deep-orange coloured precipitate when mixed with 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine (2,4-DNP) solution. A ketone has a carbonyl carbon attached to two carbon groups.

q: Carboxylic acids evolve $CO_2$ when mixed with saturated $NaHCO_3$ solution.
e: True. Carboxylic acids evolve CO2 when mixed with saturated NaHCO3 solution. Carboxylic acids contain the -COOH group and are typically weak acids.

q: Esters show decolourisation when heated gently with EtOH, phenolphthalein and dilute NaOH.
e: True. Esters show decolourisation when heated gently with EtOH, phenolphthalein and dilute NaOH. An ester has the -COO- link and is often made from an acid plus an alcohol.

q: Primary amines react with $CHCl_3$ in the presence of alkali to produce an unpleasant smell.
e: True. Primary amines react with CHCl3 in the presence of alkali to produce an unpleasant smell. An amine is an organic base with nitrogen that can accept a proton.

q: The presence of a carbonyl group such as aldehyde or ketone can be easily tested by using a solution of 2,4-DNP.
e: True. The presence of a carbonyl group such as aldehyde or ketone can be easily tested by using a solution of 2,4-DNP. An aldehyde has a carbonyl carbon attached to at least one hydrogen.

q: Fehling's solution is an acidic solution containing copper(II) ions.
e: False. Fehling's solution is alkaline copper(II). The alkaline tartrate complex is required for the test.

q: When the clear blue Fehling's solution is warmed with an aldehyde, a reddish-brown precipitate is formed.
e: True. When the clear blue Fehling's solution is warmed with an aldehyde, a reddish-brown precipitate is formed. An aldehyde has a carbonyl carbon attached to at least one hydrogen.

q: A ketone gives a reddish-brown precipitate with Fehling's solution.
e: False. Ketones do not reduce Fehling's reagent. Aldehydes give the red Cu2O precipitate.

q: Infrared (IR) spectroscopy is the study of the absorption of light by a compound, in the infrared region of the electromagnetic spectrum.
e: True. Infrared (IR) spectroscopy is the study of the absorption of light by a compound, in the infrared region of the electromagnetic spectrum. Infrared spectroscopy identifies bonds from the frequencies they absorb as they vibrate.

q:
The relationship between the energy and the frequency of electromagnetic radiation is described by Planck's equation, $E = h
u$.
e: True. The relationship between the energy and the frequency of electromagnetic radiation is described by Planck's equation, E = h u. Frequency is how many wave crests pass a point each second.

q: Wavenumber, measured in $cm^{-1}$, is the reciprocal of the wavelength and is commonly used in infrared spectroscopy.
e: True. Wavenumber, measured in cm-1, is the reciprocal of the wavelength and is commonly used in infrared spectroscopy. Infrared spectroscopy identifies bonds from the frequencies they absorb as they vibrate.

q: High frequencies, large wavenumbers, and short wavelengths are associated with low energies.
e: False. High frequency, large wavenumber, and short wavelength mean high photon energy. Low energy is the opposite end of the spectrum.

q: Photons in the infrared radiation region can cause bond vibrations in molecules.
e: True. Photons in the infrared radiation region can cause bond vibrations in molecules. Infrared spectroscopy identifies bonds from the frequencies they absorb as they vibrate.

q: Stretching is a vibration that occurs between two bonds and changes the bond angle.
e: False. Stretching changes bond length. Changing the bond angle is bending, or scissoring.

q: Only those stretching and bending motions that change the dipole moment of a molecule give rise to the absorption of infrared radiation.
e: True. Only those stretching and bending motions that change the dipole moment of a molecule give rise to the absorption of infrared radiation. Infrared spectroscopy identifies bonds from the frequencies they absorb as they vibrate.

q: Homonuclear diatomic molecules like $N_2$ which have no dipole moments are IR active.
e: False. N2 has no changing dipole when it stretches, so it is IR inactive. That is why nitrogen does not show an IR spectrum.

q: Light atoms vibrate at higher frequencies than heavier atoms and multiple bonds vibrate at higher frequencies than single bonds.
e: True. Light atoms vibrate at higher frequencies than heavier atoms and multiple bonds vibrate at higher frequencies than single bonds. The direction of this chemical relationship is the one chemists actually measure.

q: An IR spectrum is a plot of the percent transmittance or absorbance of radiation versus the wavenumber of the radiation transmitted.
e: True. An IR spectrum is a plot of the percent transmittance or absorbance of radiation versus the wavenumber of the radiation transmitted. Wavenumber counts how many waves fit into one centimetre.

q: The C=O stretching vibration in amides, ketones, aldehydes, esters, and carboxylic acids appears in the $1650-1750$ $cm^{-1}$ range and is strong and sharp.
e: True. The C=O stretching vibration in amides, ketones, aldehydes, esters, and carboxylic acids appears in the 1650-1750 cm-1 range and is strong and sharp. An aldehyde has a carbonyl carbon attached to at least one hydrogen.

q: The O-H bond of carboxylic acids usually has an absorption in the range of $3200-3600$ $cm^{-1}$.
e: False. Acid O-H is a very broad band near 2500-3300 cm^-1 because of hydrogen bonding. 3200-3600 cm^-1 is the usual alcohol or phenol O-H region.

q: The polar O-H bond usually shows strong and broad absorption bands due to the hydrogen bonding of the OH groups between molecules.
e: True. The polar O-H bond usually shows strong and broad absorption bands due to the hydrogen bonding of the OH groups between molecules. Hydrogen bonding is H on N, O, or F pulling toward another N, O, or F.

q: N-H stretches in amine and amide show up in the same wavenumber region as O-H stretches but are narrow and weak.
e: True. N-H stretches in amine and amide show up in the same wavenumber region as O-H stretches but are narrow and weak. An amine is an organic base with nitrogen that can accept a proton.
